NS-001.root_cause: VLAN 20 does not exist in the switch VLAN database, but Fa0/3 is configured as an access port in VLAN 20. The port is up and the link is good, yet frames are dropped because they are assigned to an inactive VLAN.
evidence: 1    default                          active    Fa0/1, Fa0/2, Fa0/4, Fa0/5
fix_steps: On SW1: configure terminal
Create the missing VLAN: vlan 20
Name it for clarity: name SALES-VLAN20
Exit config and confirm with: show vlan brief
Re-test the ping from PC1 to 192.168.20.1

NS-002.root_cause: PC5 is leasing from the wrong DHCP scope. The DHCP server at 192.168.30.1 is answering the request and handing out a Guest-subnet address, so the DHCP scope selection is misconfigured for this client.
fix_steps: On the router: configure terminal
Inspect the pool serving VLAN 30: show running-config | section dhcp
Reserve PC5's MAC in the Sales pool so it leases from 192.168.20.0/24
Release and renew on PC5: ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew

NS-003.root_cause: VLAN 40 is not in the allowed VLAN list on the Gi0/1 trunk. The trunk carries 1,10,20,30 only, so VLAN 40 frames are pruned at the inter-switch link even though the VLAN exists and is active on both switches.
fix_steps: On SW1: configure terminal
Select the trunk: interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Add VLAN 40 to the allowed list: switchport trunk allowed vlan add 40
Repeat on SW2 Gi0/1 - the allowed list is per-port and must match on both ends
Verify with: show interfaces trunk
secondary_findings: SW2's trunk allowed-VLAN list was not supplied. If VLAN 40 is pruned there as well, fixing only SW1 will not restore connectivity.

NS-004.root_cause: Native VLAN mismatch on the Fa0/24 trunk: SW1 uses native VLAN 1 while SW2 uses native VLAN 99. Untagged frames are placed into different VLANs at each end, which leaks traffic between VLAN 1 and VLAN 99 and makes spanning-tree behaviour inconsistent.
evidence: %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH: Native VLAN mismatch discovered on FastEthernet0/24 (1),
fix_steps: Decide which native VLAN is intended - the topology note names VLAN 99 as management, so align SW1 to 99
On SW1: configure terminal
interface FastEthernet0/24
switchport trunk native vlan 99
Confirm the CDP warning stops and verify with: show interfaces trunk
secondary_findings: Using the management VLAN as the native VLAN is workable but not best practice. A dedicated unused native VLAN would reduce the exposure of untagged traffic.

NS-005.root_cause: The inter-switch link on Gi0/1 was left in static access mode in VLAN 1 rather than configured as an 802.1q trunk. show interfaces trunk returns nothing at all, which means no trunk exists on this switch, so only VLAN 1 traffic crosses the link.
fix_steps: On SW1: configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
switchport mode trunk
Remove portfast from the trunk - it is intended for access ports: no spanning-tree portfast
Apply the same trunk configuration to SW2 Gi0/1, then verify: show interfaces trunk
secondary_findings: spanning-tree portfast is configured on what should be a switch-to-switch link. On a trunk this bypasses the listening and learning states and can create a temporary forwarding loop.

NS-006.root_cause: PC2's default gateway is set to 192.168.10.254, but no device holds that address. R1's LAN interface is 192.168.10.1, which is why PC2 can ping the router directly yet has no working gateway for off-subnet traffic.
fix_steps: On PC2, open the IP configuration
Change the default gateway from 192.168.10.254 to 192.168.10.1
Clear the stale ARP entry: arp -d 192.168.10.254
Re-test off-subnet reachability: ping 192.168.20.10
secondary_findings: If PC2 is a DHCP client, correcting it locally will be overwritten at the next renewal. Check the pool's default-router statement before closing this out.

NS-007.root_cause: The default gateway 192.168.11.1 lies outside PC3's own 192.168.10.0/24 subnet. The host cannot ARP for an address it does not consider local, so the stack fails the send outright rather than timing out.
fix_steps: On PC3, open the IP configuration
Change the default gateway from 192.168.11.1 to 192.168.10.1
Confirm the subnet mask stays 255.255.255.0
Verify: ping 192.168.10.1 then ping a host in another subnet

NS-008.root_cause: No ip default-gateway is configured on SW3. The include filter for default-gateway returns nothing, so the switch has no next hop for traffic it originates. It reaches 10.0.99.1 because that is on its own directly connected VLAN 99 subnet, and fails to 10.0.50.20 because that is off-net.
fix_steps: On SW3: configure terminal
Add a default route toward the gateway: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.99.1
Verify with: show ip route
Re-test: ping 10.0.50.20

NS-009.root_cause: The router-on-a-stick configuration has no Gi0/0.30 subinterface. Subinterfaces exist for VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 only, so VLAN 30 has no Layer 3 gateway despite the VLAN being permitted on the trunk.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.30
encapsulation dot1Q 30
Verify it comes up: show ip interface brief | include 0/0.30
Re-test from a VLAN 30 host: ping 192.168.30.1
secondary_findings: The trunk already permits VLAN 30, so the Layer 2 path is intact. Only the Layer 3 gateway is missing - no switch-side change should be needed.

NS-010.root_cause: The DHCP pool is fully exhausted. All 244 usable addresses are leased, so clients booting later get no DHCPOFFER and fall back to APIPA self-assignment in 169.254.0.0/16.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
Free the pool immediately: clear ip dhcp binding *
Shorten the lease so stale bindings recycle faster: ip dhcp pool LAB_POOL then lease 0 2
Verify utilisation drops: show ip dhcp pool
secondary_findings: A /24 with 244 usable addresses is at its structural ceiling. If the lab genuinely needs more concurrent hosts, the subnet itself must be enlarged rather than the pool retuned.

NS-011.root_cause: The DHCP pool's network statement is 192.168.99.0/24 while the serving interface Gi0/0 is 192.168.10.1/24. The router hands out addresses from a subnet that does not exist on the wire, so clients are unreachable in both directions.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
ip dhcp pool LAN_POOL
Correct the network statement: network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
Clear the wrong-subnet leases: clear ip dhcp binding *
Renew on a client and confirm it lands in 192.168.10.0/24

NS-012.root_cause: Every host has an incorrect default gateway of 192.168.10.254. Because the gateway address does not resolve to a router interface, off-subnet traffic is never forwarded, which is why intra-subnet pings succeed.
fix_steps: On each affected PC, open the IP configuration
Change the default gateway to 192.168.10.1
Clear the stale ARP entry: arp -d 192.168.10.254
Re-test off-subnet reachability

NS-013.root_cause: Gi0/0.20 has no ip helper-address, so DHCPDISCOVER broadcasts from VLAN 20 are never relayed to the server at 192.168.10.5. VLAN 10 works because its clients share a broadcast domain with the server and need no relay.
evidence: DHCPD: no DHCPDISCOVER received from GigabitEthernet0/0.20.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
ip helper-address 192.168.10.5
Verify: show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
Renew on a VLAN 20 client and confirm it leases in 192.168.20.0/24
secondary_findings: Confirm the DHCP server actually has a scope defined for 192.168.20.0/24. Relaying the broadcast to a server with no matching scope will still produce no lease.

NS-014.root_cause: The host is configured with DNS server 192.168.10.53, but nothing answers at that address. The real DNS service runs on 192.168.10.5 per the topology note, so every lookup times out while IP connectivity is unaffected.
evidence: DNS request timed out. (timeout was 2 seconds)
fix_steps: On PC1, open the IP configuration
Change the DNS server from 192.168.10.53 to 192.168.10.5
Flush the resolver cache: ipconfig /flushdns
Verify: nslookup www.lab.local

NS-015.root_cause: The DNS service is administratively disabled on the server. The host is reachable and the resource records are intact, so the daemon simply is not listening - which explains a lab-wide resolution failure with no impact on IP connectivity.
fix_steps: Open the DNS server's Services > DNS panel
Set DNS Service to On
Confirm both A records are still present after the service starts
From PC1: ipconfig /flushdns then nslookup www.lab.local
secondary_findings: A single DNS server is a single point of failure for the whole lab. A secondary resolver would keep name resolution working through this class of outage.

NS-016.root_cause: The A record for www.lab.local points to 192.168.20.99, which is not assigned to any host. Resolution succeeds and returns that address, then the connection attempt goes nowhere. The actual web server is 192.168.20.10.
fix_steps: Open the DNS server's Services > DNS panel
Edit the www.lab.local A record to 192.168.20.10
Save the record and confirm DNS Service is still On
On PC1: ipconfig /flushdns then nslookup www.lab.local
Browse to http://www.lab.local to confirm end to end

NS-017.root_cause: R1 has no route to 192.168.30.0/24 and no default route. Its table holds only the two directly connected networks, so it drops the traffic itself and returns an ICMP unreachable - which is why the reply comes from the gateway address rather than timing out.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
Verify it installed: show ip route static
Confirm R2 has a return route to 192.168.10.0/24 before declaring this fixed
Re-test end to end from PC1
secondary_findings: R2's routing table was not supplied. A missing return route on R2 would produce the same user-visible symptom and should be checked in the same pass.

NS-018.root_cause: The static route to 10.10.30.0/24 points at next hop 10.0.0.9, which does not exist. On a /30 link the only valid peer address is 10.0.0.2, and CDP confirms that is the actual neighbour. IOS installs a static route without validating the next hop, which is why the route appears healthy while traffic fails.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
Remove the bad route: no ip route 10.10.30.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.9
Add the correct one: ip route 10.10.30.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.2
Verify: show ip route static
Re-test: ping 10.10.30.1 source GigabitEthernet0/1
secondary_findings: 10.0.0.9 is not even inside the 10.0.0.0/30 subnet configured on Gi0/1, so this was a typo rather than a valid-but-wrong peer. Worth checking whether other static routes on this router share the same mistake.

NS-019.root_cause: R1 has no default route toward the ISP. The table contains the two LANs and the WAN transit network but no 0.0.0.0/0 entry, so packets for internet destinations have no matching route and R1 answers with an ICMP unreachable even though the ISP next hop is pingable.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
Verify the gateway of last resort is set: show ip route
Re-test from R1: ping 8.8.8.8
Then re-test from PC1 - if the router succeeds but the host does not, NAT is the next thing to check
secondary_findings: Internal hosts use RFC1918 addressing, so a default route alone will not give them internet access without NAT. Verify ip nat inside/outside and the translation rule in the same pass.

NS-020.root_cause: The shared 10.0.0.0/30 link is placed in OSPF area 0 on R1 and area 1 on R2. Area IDs must match on a common segment, so the hello packets are discarded and no adjacency forms - which is why the neighbour table is empty despite full IP reachability.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
router ospf 1
Remove the area 0 statement: no network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
Re-add it in area 1 to match R2: network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 1
Verify the neighbour forms: show ip ospf neighbor

NS-021.root_cause: The route to 192.168.20.0/24 is present and correct, and 192.168.20.50 responds normally over it. The hosts from .70 upward are most likely powered off or running a local firewall that drops ICMP echo requests, since the forwarding path itself is demonstrably working.
fix_steps: Confirm 192.168.20.80 is powered on and connected
Check for a host firewall blocking ICMP on the affected machines
From R2, ping 192.168.20.80 locally to confirm it answers on its own segment
If R2 can reach it locally, investigate the return path from R2 toward 192.168.10.0/24

NS-022.root_cause: ACL 101 is applied outbound on Gi0/0, the LAN-facing interface. In that direction it inspects traffic being delivered to the LAN rather than traffic sourced from it, so the permit for LAN-to-server never matches and the deny at sequence 20 drops all returning traffic.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
Remove the outbound application: no ip access-group 101 out
Apply it inbound instead: ip access-group 101 in
Watch the counters move onto sequence 10: show access-lists 101
secondary_findings: Once applied inbound, the deny at sequence 20 will still block DNS and DHCP for the LAN. If the intent is HTTP-only to the server, that is correct; if general internet access is expected, ACL 101 needs additional permits.

NS-023.root_cause: ACL entry ordering is wrong. The broad deny at sequence 10 covers the whole 192.168.10.0/24 source range to the server, so it matches 192.168.10.20 first and the specific permit at sequence 20 is never evaluated. The 417 matches on the deny and 0 on the permit confirm the shadowing.
evidence: 20 permit tcp host 192.168.10.20 host 192.168.20.10 eq www (0 matches)
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
ip access-list extended 110
Remove the shadowed permit: no 20
Re-insert it ahead of the deny: 5 permit tcp host 192.168.10.20 host 192.168.20.10 eq www
Verify the order and watch sequence 5 take matches: show access-lists 110

NS-024.root_cause: ACL 120 permits only TCP 80 and 443. Everything else falls through to the implicit deny ip any any at the end of the list, which silently drops UDP 53 for DNS and UDP 67/68 for DHCP. Web browsing survives because it is the only thing explicitly permitted.
evidence: 10 permit tcp any any eq www (2043 matches)
20 permit tcp any any eq 443 (1877 matches)
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
ip access-list extended 120
Permit name resolution: 30 permit udp any host 192.168.10.5 eq domain
Re-test: nslookup www.lab.local and ipconfig /renew
Verify the new entry is taking matches: show access-lists 120
secondary_findings: The implicit deny also blocks ICMP, so ping-based troubleshooting from these hosts will keep failing until an explicit permit is added.

NS-025.root_cause: The deny entry in GUEST_FILTER has its source and destination reversed. It reads deny ip 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255, which on the interface where it is applied evaluates guest-destined rather than guest-sourced traffic, so guest-to-internal flows fall through to the permit at sequence 20.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
ip access-list extended GUEST_FILTER
Remove the reversed entry: no 10
Re-add with source and destination swapped: 10 deny ip 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255
Re-test from the guest host and confirm the deny takes matches

NS-026.root_cause: Neither interface carries an ip nat inside or ip nat outside designation. The translation rule and its source ACL both exist, but NAT never engages without interface roles, so internal traffic leaves with its RFC1918 source address and is discarded upstream. The empty interface lists in show ip nat statistics prove it.
evidence: ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0 then ip nat inside
interface GigabitEthernet0/1 then ip nat outside
Verify both lists are now populated: show ip nat statistics
Generate traffic from a LAN host and confirm entries appear in: show ip nat translations
secondary_findings: Hits: 0 Misses: 0 means no traffic has even been offered to the NAT process. If the counters stay at zero after applying the roles, the problem is upstream of NAT - check for a default route first.

NS-027.root_cause: The NAT source ACL permits only 192.168.10.0/24. VLAN 20 traffic is marked ip nat inside on the subinterface but never matches access-list 1, so it leaves the router untranslated with a private source address and is dropped by the ISP.
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
Add the missing source network: access-list 1 permit 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255
Confirm both lines are present: show running-config | include access-list 1
Generate traffic from a VLAN 20 host
Confirm a 192.168.20.x entry appears in: show ip nat translations
secondary_findings: Standard ACL 1 is being reused as a NAT selector. Converting it to a named ACL would make the intent clearer and avoid a later collision if ACL 1 is also used for filtering.

NS-028.root_cause: The overload keyword is missing from the NAT statement, so the router performs one-to-one dynamic NAT instead of PAT. With 203.0.113.2 as the only public address, exactly one internal host can hold a translation at a time, and the next host displaces it.
evidence: ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Total active translations: 1 (0 static, 1 dynamic; 0 extended)
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
Remove the non-overloaded rule: no ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Re-add it with PAT: ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
Clear existing translations: clear ip nat translation *
Browse from two hosts at once and confirm both appear in: show ip nat translations
secondary_findings: 0 extended translations in the statistics output is the same signal seen from another angle - PAT produces extended entries with port numbers, plain NAT does not.

NS-029.root_cause: The LAB-GUEST SSID is mapped to VLAN 10, the internal VLAN, rather than guest VLAN 50. Guests are placed directly onto the internal subnet, so GUEST_FILTER on the 192.168.50.0/24 boundary is never in the traffic path at all - its 0 matches confirm it is being bypassed rather than failing.
NS-029.next_command: show running-config | section dot11 ssid LAB-GUEST
fix_steps: Treat this as an active security incident before it is a config fault - guests currently have internal access
On the WLC/AP, open Wireless > WLANs and select LAB-GUEST
Change the Interface/VLAN mapping from VLAN 10 to VLAN 50
Confirm VLAN 50 is permitted on the AP-to-switch trunk and that Gi0/0.50 has a DHCP scope
Reconnect a guest client and verify it lands in 192.168.50.0/24
Confirm GUEST_FILTER starts taking matches, which proves guest traffic is now being evaluated
secondary_findings: Client isolation is Disabled on the guest SSID. Even after the VLAN is corrected, guests will be able to reach each other directly.
Any device that connected to LAB-GUEST while it was mapped to VLAN 10 held an internal address. The DHCP bindings for 192.168.10.0/24 should be audited rather than assumed clean.

NS-030.root_cause: Security mode mismatch between AP and client. AP1 runs WPA2-PSK with AES while LAPTOP1 is configured for WEP. The two authentication methods are not interoperable, so association fails and the client re-prompts for credentials that would never be accepted regardless of correctness.
fix_steps: On LAPTOP1, open Config > Wireless0
Change Authentication from WEP to WPA2-PSK
Set encryption to AES to match the AP
Enter the passphrase Cisco12345
Confirm association: show dot11 associations on AP1
secondary_findings: Fix the client rather than the AP. Downgrading AP1 to WEP would also resolve the symptom but WEP is cryptographically broken and would weaken every other client on the SSID.

NS-031.root_cause: The WPA2-PSK key exchange is failing intermittently on the LAB-IOT SSID. Clients reach the association stage but the four-way handshake does not complete cleanly, so the DHCP exchange never gets through and the client self-assigns an APIPA address.
fix_steps: On AP2, open Wireless > WLANs and select LAB-IOT
Re-enter the WPA2-PSK passphrase to rule out a corrupted key
Save and let the clients re-associate
Confirm clients obtain a routable address

NS-032.root_cause: R1 Gi0/1 is in a shutdown state. The interface reports administratively down, which is set by configuration rather than caused by cabling, so no amount of reseating will bring it up. R2's side shows up/down because it has carrier at its own port but no protocol peer.
evidence: GigabitEthernet0/1     10.0.0.1        YES manual administratively down down
GigabitEthernet0/1 is administratively down, line protocol is down (disabled)
fix_steps: On R1: configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
no shutdown
Confirm both status and protocol read up: show ip interface brief
Verify the peer: ping 10.0.0.2
secondary_findings: R2 Gi0/1 shows up/down, which is consistent with a shut peer and needs no separate fix. Re-check it after R1 comes up rather than changing it now.

NS-033.root_cause: Duplex mismatch on the Gi0/2 uplink. SW1 is hard-set to full-duplex, which is the misconfigured end, while SW2 correctly negotiated half-duplex. In full-duplex mode SW1 transmits without carrier sense, colliding with SW2's traffic - hence the input errors on SW1 and the late collisions on SW2.
fix_steps: On SW1: configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
Set the port to half-duplex to match SW2: duplex half
Clear the counters and confirm errors stop rising: clear counters GigabitEthernet0/2
Re-test a large file transfer between buildings
secondary_findings: Ping succeeds throughout because small, infrequent packets rarely collide. This is why a duplex mismatch presents as a throughput problem rather than a reachability one.
